Maladaptive Strategies.value: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being alone in a room or building
Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events

Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The people responsible have faced no consequences
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, nocturnal checking for one's own immediate physical safety is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it introduces a more direct personal-danger threat theme that is not otherwise represented in triggers or memory. The triggers and memory items are centered on reminders of the loved one's trauma/loss rather than the patient's own current physical danger, so this specific item is the least coherent threat item.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character can occur after a loved one's trauma, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals focused on institutional failure and lack of accountability, which externalize blame to others. This is not impossible, but this item is the most internally tensioned within the appraisal node and less clearly linked to the rest of the profile than guilt on recall would be.

vignette:
Karim's Story

Karim Mansouri was fifty-two when his daughter Layla died. She was seven years old, struck by a car in the parking lot of a suburban mall on a Tuesday afternoon in March. His ex-wife had been watching her-they had shared custody, and Karim had been in Los Angeles for a film shoot, a supporting role in a television drama that required him to be present on set from dawn until well past dinner. When the call came, he was in his trailer, running lines for a scene he would film the next morning. He did not remember driving to the hospital. He remembered the fluorescent lights, the smell of antiseptic, and the peculiar silence of his ex-wife's face as she told him that Layla had not survived surgery.

The driver had not been charged. The police report concluded it was an accident-a momentary lapse of attention at a low speed, a child who had darted from between parked cars. No one was held accountable. Karim had come to believe, with a certainty that felt almost physical, that the mall's security should have been better, that the parking lot design was negligent, that someone in authority should have been forced to answer for the conditions that made such a death possible. But no one had. The driver received a citation for failure to yield. Karim received a daughter who no longer existed.

In the months that followed, Karim could not reconcile his inaction with the fact of her death. He had been on a soundstage, memorizing dialogue about fictional troubles, while Layla was in a parking lot with a distracted driver. He had not been there. He had not protected her. He would never forgive himself for not doing more-though what more he could have done from three hundred miles away remained a torment he could not articulate. The guilt was not a feeling that came and went; it was a permanent weight he carried, one that intensified whenever he allowed himself to remember the shape of her face or the particular way she had laughed at his impressions.

The memories themselves came to him in disconnected fragments. He could see her hand reaching for his in the parking lot of a different mall, years earlier. He could see the hospital waiting room, though he was not certain he had actually been in that room or had only imagined it afterward. He could see, with photographic clarity, the face of the police officer who had handed him a tissue. But these images did not cohere into a coherent narrative; they floated in his mind like photographs scattered on a table, and his mind could not arrange them into a story that made sense.

By the time Karim sought help, eighteen months had passed. His career had contracted significantly. He found himself unable to concentrate on scripts; the words would blur on the page, and his mind would splinter into those fragmented images. He had turned down roles, claiming illness, and then had begun accepting any part offered to him, no matter how small or demeaning, because saying no to anything felt dangerous. If he refused work, he would be alone in his apartment. If he was alone, the silence would be absolute, and in that silence, the memories would sharpen.

He avoided crowds now. Shopping centers were impossible-the sound of children playing in the mall's common areas would send him into a state of near-panic, his chest tightening, his breath coming in shallow gasps. He had stopped going to restaurants during busy hours. He attended his few remaining auditions and then left immediately, driving aimlessly until evening, when he might reasonably return to a public place-a diner, a bookstore, anywhere that was not empty.

What frightened him most was that even when his few remaining friends assured him he was safe, that his presence at a location would not cause harm, he could not believe them. The world had shown him that safety was an illusion, that a child could be taken in an instant, that institutions would fail and no one would answer for it. He had come to see danger everywhere, particularly in the spaces between people, in the moments when he was unwatched and unaccountable himself.

When Karim finally made the call to a therapist, it was because he had realized he was disappearing. Not dying-disappearing. He was becoming smaller, more constrained, more apologetic for existing. He went along with whatever others wanted, saying yes to auditions he dreaded and no to activities that might have brought him peace, all to avoid the terror of his own solitude. He was afraid that if he stopped moving, stopped performing, stopped trying to keep himself safe through compliance, he would finally have to face the fact that he had not been there when it mattered, and that no amount of guilt or memory or avoidance would change that.
